title: Child marriage before and after the 2019 ban in Brazil: An interrupted time series analysis
content:
by Marcelo Luis Urquia, Maria Paula Godoy, Carolina Fonseca Leal de Araújo, Carla Adriane Leal de Araújo, José Roberto da Silva Junior, João Guilherme Bezerra Alves

Background

Child marriage, defined as a legal marriage or informal union of a minor, is considered a violation to human rights and is associated with adverse developmental and health outcomes. Brazil is one of the countries with the highest number of child marriages worldwide. In 2019, Brazil enacted legislation banning child marriage for <16-year-olds. We examined the time trends in child marriage before and after the law and contextualized them within those of adolescents and young adults up to 24 years of age.

Methods

We accessed public-use anonymized marriage and birth registrations nationwide data in the period 2014–2024, with complete information on age and marital status. To describe the trends before and after the law reform, we used interrupted time series analysis. Analyses were stratified by age (<16, 16–17, 18–19 and 20–24 years), marital status (legally married and informal unions) and sex.

Results

From 2014 to 2019, civil marriage registrations among boys and girls and births to legally married and in union minor mothers exhibited a significant downward trend. Marriages among <16-year-old children were expected to zero out shortly after 2019, but they did not. Marriages and births to married mothers decelerated after 2019 in all age groups. Trends in the proportion of births to mothers in informal unions remained unaffected across all age groups.

Conclusions

Despite decreasing historical trends, the new law was not associated with a reduction in legal marriages or informal unions among <16-year-olds. The deceleration in legal marriages across all age groups after 2019 suggests that broader societal influences, including a potential impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, may have been at play. Additional legal and social interventions are needed to address child marriage in Brazil.
author: Marcelo Luis Urquia
